senses: One who plays the lute, a lutist.
ety: Borrowed from Medieval Latin lutanista, from lutana (“lute”), from Middle French lut. By surface analysis, lute + -n- + -ist.

senses: A thin, crisp, salted, customarily white-colored cracker; a soda cracker; a soda biscuit.
ety: Genericized trademark. Originally a US brand name in the late 1800s, presumably salt + -ine.

senses: Any member of a class of molluscs (Gastropoda) that includes snails, slugs, and limpets; univalve mollusc.
ety: From French gastéropode, from gastro- + -poda, New Latin, from Ancient Greek γαστήρ (gastḗr, “stomach”) and πούς (poús, “foot”).

senses: The doctrine, theory, or metaphysics of monads.
ety: From monad + -ology.
examples: Heidegger reposited the question which had earlier been posited by the doctor of monadology, Leibnitz.

senses: A wrinkle or crease.
ety: From Middle English runkel (“wrinkle, crease”). Cognate with Scots runkil (“wrinkle, crease”). Of uncertain origin, perhaps from a diminutive ( + -le) of Old Norse *hrunka, hrukka (“wrinkle”), from Proto-Germanic *hrunkwǭ (“wrinkle”). The verb is from Middle English runklen (“to wrinkle”), from the noun. Compare also Old Swedish rynkia (whence Swedish rynka (“to wrinkle”)).

senses: Associated with or tending to cause deflation.
ety: From deflation + -ary.

senses: A kind of spring roll.
ety: (Philippines): Borrowed from Tagalog lumpia, from Hokkien 潤餅 /润饼 (lūn-piáⁿ). (Indonesia): Borrowed from Indonesian lumpia, inherited from Malay lumpia, from Hokkien 潤餅 /润饼 (lūn-piáⁿ). Compare Spanish lumpiá, Dutch loempia, Cebuano lumpya.

senses: A semiaquatic rodent of the tribe Ondatrini.
Any of several shrews in the family Soricidae, especially an Asian house shrew (Suncus murinus).
ety: Perhaps so called for its musky odour and because it resembles a rat, or perhaps called by an Algonquian name like the Abenaki moskwas, with the spelling altered under the influence of the English words musk and rat.

senses: Having no polarity.
ety: From a- + polar.

senses: A type of sushi made from freshwater eel.
ety: Borrowed from Japanese 鰻 (unagi, “eel”).

senses: The care and treatment of the eyes.
ety: From eye + care.

senses: The process of assembling or bringing together.
A collection of things which have been gathered together or assembled.
A gathering of people.
A group of different artifacts found in association with one another.
A visual art form similar to collage, which combines two-dimensional and three-dimensional, often found, elements into works of art.
ety: Borrowed from French assemblage. By surface analysis, assemble + -age.

senses: The plinth, or lowest member, of any pedestal, podium, water table, or the like.
A fillet, or listel.
A frame enclosing a bas relief.
ety: Borrowed from Latin quadra.

senses: The protection of humans against bioweapons, or from the accidental release of biohazards.
ety: From bio- + security.

senses: A liquid crystal whose molecules align in loose parallel lines.
ety: From Ancient Greek νήματος (nḗmatos), genitive of νῆμα (nêma, “thread”).
examples: It is easy to see, however, that the same coefficients in nematics determine the adiabatic deformations also.
For low-molecular-weight nematics, it has been known that the constitutive equation of nematics is entirely different from that for isotropic liquids.

Electrohydrodynamic instabilities in nematics could be classified according to the dependence of the threshold voltage (or field) on the physical parameters of the liquid crystal, cell geometry, field frequency, etc.

senses: A lively style of music originating from India.
A traditional Punjabi folk dance, originally a celebration of the harvest.
Any style of electronic dance music (EDM) influenced by the musics of the Indian subcontinent.
A false daisy (Eclipta prostrata).
ety: From Punjabi ਭੰਗੜਾ (bhaṅgṛā) / بَھن٘گْڑا (bhaṉgṛā), from ਭੰਗ / بَھن٘گ (bhaṉg, “hemp”) + ـڑا (-ṛā).

senses: The seating section of a Greek or Roman theatre or amphitheatre.
ety: Learned borrowing from Latin cavea. Doublet of cage.
examples: No rib foundation appears ever to have been designed for subterranean vaulting like that commonly found elsewhere in Roman caveas to support seating.
As the entrances near the caveas provide access to the theatres, such an additional arrangement seems to have been superfluous.
And they claimed in the caveas of their theatres that we (the Greeks, I mean) are supposedly no one’s subjugated slaves.

senses: An electronic device that samples a varying quantity (e.g. a waveform) and generates a digital response
ety: From quantize + -er.

senses: The lipids in milk.
ety: From milk + fat.

senses: Proliferating; tending to proliferate.
ety: From proliferate + -ive.

senses: Having hide (skin) of a specified kind.
ety: From Middle English hided, equivalent to hide + -ed.

senses: Taking place offstage (as above).
ety: From off + stage.

senses: The act of formalizing something.
ety: From formal + -ization.

senses: A musician who plays the organ.
ety: From Middle French organiste, from Medieval Latin organista. By surface analysis, organ + -ist.

senses: A mayflower or trailing arbutus (Epigaea repens).
Arbute; wood of strawberry trees.
ety: From taxonomic name Arbutus, from Latin arbutus.

senses: A hearth, stove, or other traditional cooking-place.
ety: From Hindi चूल्हा (cūlhā), Bengali চুলা (cula).
examples: When the basket was full, she carried it back and emptied it next to the outdoor chula where she did most of her cooking.

senses: Extractivist practices in the management of natural resources.
ety: From extractive + -ism, originally applied to mining practices in Latin America.
examples: Industrial extractivism (a definition that Vidal would extend to include modern intensive agriculture) has contributed to the recent freefall in bird, mammal and amphibian numbers.

senses: Having tentacles.
ety: From tentacle + -ed.
examples: The eight-tentacled octopus swam through the water.

senses: A strip on a TAB (tape automated bonding) chip where components are attached by using a reflow head to hold them down while applying pressure and pulse heat to form a bond.
ety: From hot + bar.
examples: Frequently, if a contact preparation between an unknown and an easily supercooled material such as thymol is allowed to digest on the hotbar, the unknown will develop well defined crystal faces in the mixing zone.
Minimum requirements for the hotbar bonding cycle are component acquisition, placement, and reflow while attached to a substrate.
Manufacturers of affordable custom hotbar bonding equipment used in chip-on-flex, chip-on-glass, or Hex (TAB) attach.

senses: The Cape petrel, Daption capense.
A guinea fowl, especially as food.
ety: From Portuguese pintado (literally “painted”).
examples: We now bore away SSE, SE & SEBS as the ice trended, keeping close by the edge of it, where we saw many penguins and whales and many of the ice birds, small grey birds and pintadoes.

senses: The act of going to or hearing a religious confession.
Confession to a priest.
ety: From Middle English shrift (“confession to a priest; act or instance of this; sacrament of penance; penance assigned by a priest; penitence, repentance; punishment for sin”) [and other forms], from Old English sċrift (“penance, shrift; something prescribed as punishment, penalty; one who passes sentence, a judge”), from sċrīfan (“of a priest: to prescribe absolution or penance; to pass judgment, ordain, prescribe; to appoint, decree”) (whence shrive), from Proto-Germanic *skrībaną (“to write”), from Latin scrībō (“to write”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kreybʰ- (“to scratch, tear”)

senses: A group or network of people involved in the production, commission, preservation, promotion, criticism, and sale of art.
ety: From art + world, popularized by art critic Arthur Danto (1924–2013), see quotations.
examples: Probably he would maintain that at least some of the regards intended for artworks are common to all the artworlds there are and that it is this feature that unifies these artworlds as of a single type.
Rather than being in conflict, it is more accurate to suggest that these institutions lack a clear understanding of how they relate to each other under the emergence of an academy artworld.

senses: Terrorism that involves biological weapons or other biological agents.
ety: From bio- + terrorism.

senses: An assembly for protecting a space telescope from solar heat.
ety: From sun + shield.

senses: A merganser, Mergus merganser, of the northern hemisphere, that consume fish and are common on lakes and rivers.
ety: Blend of goose + gander. The oldest known use is by Drayton (1622).

senses: Occurring before marriage; antenuptial.
ety: From pre- + nuptial.

senses: A (pre-mixed) alcoholic drink containing rum and a fruit flavor like orange.
A school of fish that swim near the surface of the water, causing ripples that look similar to those caused by a light breeze on still water.
A vertical pipe attached to a septic system's distribution pipe that rises above the ground to provide ventilation.
A window with horizontal openings, designed for ventilation.
An open-air trolley.
ety: From breeze + -er, the drink originated as a brand name: Bacardi Breezer.
examples: A large proportion reported on having drunk beer, wine, cider or breezers than having consumed spirits.

A few years ago the breezer was introduced in the Dutch markets. A breezer contains a considerable amount of pure alcohol. Among young people it became the rage to drink a few breezers during a party or in a pub.
The Adjutant very lovingly called him to his side and said “So you want to give him a breezer, eh? Advocating alcohol in the academy eh?

senses: Shaking uncontrollably, especially due to fear or awe; trembling or shivering.
ety: From Middle English quakynge, quakand, from Old English cwaciende (“quaking”), present participle of Old English cwacian (“to quake, tremble”); equivalent to quake + -ing.

senses: A bright red colour tinted with orange.
Synonym of dragon's blood (“type of resin”).
ety: First attested in the mid-15th century. From Middle English cynabare, from Old French cinabre, from Latin cinnabaris, from Ancient Greek κιννάβαρι (kinnábari), of unknown origin.

senses: One who suffers from agoraphobia.
ety: From agora- + -phobic, see agoraphobia.
